status_summary: No federal law or executive action found in this review prohibits pornography in general, imprisons its producers and distributors as a class, registers educators or librarians as sex offenders for providing it, or shuts down technology firms for hosting it. The closest step is a pair of bills: on 2025-05-08 Sen. Mike Lee introduced S. 1671 and Rep. Mary Miller introduced H.R. 3297, each titled the Interstate Obscenity Definition Act, which would add a definition of obscenity for visual depictions to the Communications Act and strike the intent-to-harass element from 47 U.S.C. 223(a)(1)(A); the texts refer them to the Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee and the House Energy and Commerce Committee, and the sponsor presents the bills as making obscene material, including pornography, easier to prosecute across state lines. This review found no reported committee or floor action on either bill. Adjacent actions are narrower. The Take It Down Act (Public Law 119-12, approved 2025-05-19) makes it a federal crime to publish intimate images of an identifiable person without consent, including computer-generated forgeries, and required covered platforms to run a 48-hour removal process by 2026-05-19 under FTC enforcement. On 2025-06-27 the Supreme Court held in Free Speech Coalition v. Paxton that Texas may require age verification for sites with material harmful to minors, applying intermediate scrutiny.

timeline.event: Sen. Mike Lee (S. 1671) and Rep. Mary Miller (H.R. 3297) introduce the Interstate Obscenity Definition Act. The bill text adds a definition of obscenity for visual depictions to section 3 of the Communications Act (prurient interest, sexual acts or lewd exhibition with intent to arouse, lack of serious value) and strikes the intent-to-harass element from 47 U.S.C. 223(a)(1)(A). The Senate bill is referred to the Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee and the House bill to Energy and Commerce. It does not ban pornography in general.

The Take It Down Act is approved as Public Law 119-12. It creates federal offenses for publishing nonconsensual intimate images and digital forgeries (up to 2 years for adult depictions, up to 3 years for minor depictions) and requires covered platforms to remove reported depictions within 48 hours, with FTC enforcement.

In Free Speech Coalition v. Paxton the Supreme Court affirms the Fifth Circuit 6 to 3 (Thomas, J.), holding that Texas H.B. 1181's age-verification requirement for sites with more than one-third sexual material harmful to minors survives intermediate scrutiny. Kagan, J., dissents, joined by Sotomayor and Jackson.
timeline.source: Supreme Court of the United States

timeline.event: The U.S. Sentencing Commission publishes proposed amendments to the Guidelines Manual to respond to the Take It Down Act (Statutory Index and the commentary to section 2A6.1), with comments due 2026-02-10.

Statutory deadline (one year after enactment) for covered platforms to put the Take It Down Act notice-and-removal process in place; the Act treats noncompliance as an FTC unfair or deceptive practice violation.

The FTC publishes a revised Privacy Act system of records notice for its consumer complaint system that covers complaints from people reporting platforms that fail to remove nonconsensual intimate images within 48 hours.
